name: conditional
title: Spanish Conditional Practice: Would, Polite Requests and Quiz
description: Practice the Spanish conditional: hablaría, comería, the 12 irregular stems, polite requests and advice, with a rule table and 10 sentences checked as you tap.
answer: The Spanish conditional means would: me gustaría, comeríamos, viviría. Add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían to the whole infinitive, the same endings for -ar, -er and -ir. A small group uses a shortened stem: tendría, podría, haría, diría, saldría, vendría, pondría, querría, sabría, habría. Use it for polite requests, advice and hypothetical situations.

demand.source: Google autocomplete for US searchers (hl=en, gl=us), docs/seo-plan/us1000/suggest-us-20261127b.csv

rules.example: tendría, podría, haría, diría, saldría, vendría
Yo que tú, estudiaría más. Deberías dormir.
Si tuviera dinero, viajaría a Perú.

quiz.after: un vaso de agua, por favor.

quiz.why: Poder has a short stem: podría.
Advice with yo que tú takes the conditional.
Hacer has the stem har-: haríamos.
Hypothetical result after si + imperfect subjunctive: conditional.
Venir has the stem vendr-: vendrían.
Decir has the stem dir-: dirías.

quiz.after: ir al concierto, pero tiene que trabajar.
quiz.why: Querer drops the e in the conditional: querría, with double r.
Saber has the stem sabr-: sabríamos.

quiz.after: más feliz en otra ciudad, ¿no crees?
quiz.why: Tú form of the conditional: serías; sería is yo or él.

mistakes: Adding the ending to the stem instead of the infinitive: «hablía» should be «hablaría».
Using regular forms for irregular stems: «tenería» should be «tendría», «poneríamos» should be «pondríamos».
Using the conditional after si: «si tendría dinero» should be «si tuviera dinero»; the conditional goes in the other half.
Forgetting the accent on the í: hablaria, comerian and viviriamos all need it.
Translating every «would» as conditional: «when I was a child, I would play outside» is a habit in the past, so it takes the imperfect: jugaba.

heritage: In speech, many heritage speakers use the conditional after si («si tendría tiempo, iría»), a pattern heard in several regions. Written Spanish and the AP exam expect «si tuviera tiempo, iría». Also check the accent on every conditional ending: comería, viviríamos.
teacher: Hand out dilemma cards (you find a wallet, you win a trip) and have students answer ¿Qué harías? in pairs. Then each reports a partner's answer with dijo que haría…

faq.question: How do you form the Spanish conditional?
faq.answer: Take the infinitive and add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos or -ían: hablar → hablaría, comer → comerías, vivir → viviríamos. The same verbs that are irregular in the future are irregular here, with the same stems.

faq.question: Is «would» always the conditional?
faq.answer: No. When «would» describes a past habit (we would go to the beach every summer), Spanish uses the imperfect: íbamos a la playa. The conditional is for hypothetical or polite meanings.

faq.question: What goes with si: conditional or subjunctive?
faq.answer: The si clause takes the imperfect subjunctive and the result takes the conditional: si tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría. Never put the conditional right after si in standard Spanish.
